kakekotoba.reading_secondary: implicit 高し (high/lofty, as in high waves)
kakekotoba.interaction: The place name Takashi-no-hama (a famous shore) resonates with 高し 'high,' reinforcing the image of waves rising high, though the primary function is toponymic; some commentators note this associative overtone but it is not a fully independent grammatical pivot.

kakekotoba.reading_secondary: adanami evokes ada (仇/徒 - fickle, faithless) applied metaphorically to a faithless lover
kakekotoba.interaction: あだ浪 literally means 'wanton/inconstant waves' but simultaneously characterizes the faithless man being warned against — the waves that carelessly wet the shore stand for his fickle advances, so 'wave' and 'faithless suitor' are fused in one word.

kakekotoba.reading_primary: kakeji (I will not let [the waves/my heart] be involved/touch)
kakekotoba.reading_secondary: kake- from 掛く 'to hang/entrust one's heart' combined with 懸けじ 'will not risk/engage'
kakekotoba.interaction: かけ carries both the sense of waves 'breaking upon/touching' the shore and of the speaker 'engaging her heart' with the man's advances — she vows not to let either happen.

kakekotoba.reading_primary: nure (to become wet, of sleeves from waves/spray)
kakekotoba.reading_secondary: nure also conventionally signifies weeping/being overcome with emotion (tears wetting sleeves)
kakekotoba.interaction: The literal wetting of sleeves by wave-spray doubles as the wetting of sleeves with tears of heartbreak, so the coastal image and the emotional consequence of a love affair are simultaneously present in one word.

jokotoba.text: 音にきく高師の浜のあだ浪は
jokotoba.function: The opening three ku build an extended image of a famous shore (Takashi-no-hama) known for its restless, faithless waves, purely by reputation ('I hear tell'), which then pivots via かけ (both 'waves breaking/touching' and 'engaging one's heart') into the speaker's resolve not to let a faithless man's advances touch her heart.

honkadori.source_poem: Man'yōshū-derived proverbial association of Takashi-no-hama with inconstant waves, echoed in earlier Kokinshū-era poems using 高師の浜のあだ波 as a stock image for a fickle lover's advances
honkadori.function: invokes the established poetic reputation of Takashi-no-hama as a place proverbially associated with restless, untrustworthy waves, transferring that reputation onto the human lover being distrusted

kigo.note: Takashi-no-hama is a famous utamakura (poetic place name) associated with waves rather than any specific season; the poem's imagery of waves and shore is conventional love-poem scenery, not seasonal. No explicit seasonal marker (blossom, snow, moon, autumn wind, dew, frost, insects, birds) appears anywhere in the text — the wave/shore imagery here functions purely as a metaphor for an inconstant lover's advances, placing this poem in the Love (恋) category rather than any of the four seasons.

bipartite.kami_theme: The famous, reputedly wanton waves of Takashi-no-hama, known only by hearsay, introduced as a scene-setting image
bipartite.shimo_theme: The speaker's resolve not to let her heart (or sleeves) be touched by a faithless man's advances, for fear of the tears/heartbreak that would follow
bipartite.pivot_note: The wave imagery of the kami-no-ku is never abandoned but transforms, via the pivot かけ, into a direct statement about the speaker's emotional guardedness — the waves that carelessly wet the shore become the metaphorical vehicle for a fickle lover's advances, and the poem's entire force rests on holding 'wave touching shore' and 'man touching my heart' as one continuous image.
